report:
## Conclusion

The evidence does **not** support the claim that this is false — the claim is actually well-supported by the best available evidence. Chlorhexidine-alcohol skin prep before cesarean delivery does reduce surgical-site infection compared with iodine-alcohol.

## Evidence

The key evidence is a large, well-conducted randomized controlled trial by Tuuli et al., published in the *New England Journal of Medicine* (2016), which directly compared chlorhexidine-alcohol to iodine-alcohol for skin antisepsis at cesarean delivery. It found chlorhexidine-alcohol produced a significantly lower risk of surgical-site infection than iodine-alcohol, with a relative risk of 0.55 (95% CI, 0.34–0.90) — roughly cutting infection risk in half (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1511048).

This finding is corroborated by subsequent systematic reviews and meta-analyses pooling multiple RCTs. One meta-analysis reported a significant reduction in SSI with chlorhexidine-alcohol versus povidone-iodine (RR 0.72; 95% CI 0.52–0.98), with no heterogeneity across studies (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30184558/). A more recent network meta-analysis of RCTs in cesarean section similarly found that alcohol-based 2% chlorhexidine had the highest probability of being the most effective antiseptic for preventing surgical-site infections, ahead of alcohol-based povidone-iodine (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0195670124001282). A Cochrane review of 13 trials involving nearly 7,000 women likewise found chlorhexidine more effective at reducing infection risk, as summarized in clinical guidance documents (https://med.uc.edu/docs/default-source/obstetrics-and-gynecology-docs/ob-mfm-protocols/q-z/surgical-site-infection-prevention-following-cesarean-delivery.pdf?sfvrsn=68ec954d_2).

Some smaller individual trials (e.g., pilot RCTs) showed favorable but not statistically significant trends toward chlorhexidine, but these do not overturn the consistent, larger body of evidence, including the pivotal RCT and multiple meta-analyses, all pointing the same direction.

**Bottom line:** The claim is accurate, not false — chlorhexidine-alcohol is superior to iodine-alcohol for reducing SSI after cesarean delivery.
